title: The Peasant and the Bear

sources.author: Valery Carrick, translated by Nevill Forbes
sources.title: More Russian Picture Tales

provenance.rights: The text is our own retelling of a traditional Russian folk tale, written for Omramo; it does not use the wording of the cited edition. The cited edition is in the US public domain (published before 1931); other territories not verified. Legal review pending (PRD Q23).

geography.lesson: Russia's great forests and the farm fields at their edge; summers in the north are short, so villagers grew root crops such as turnips, and grain such as rye.

culture.lesson: Village farming in old Russia (plough, sickle, turnips, rye and black bread), and the bear as the best-known animal of Russian tales: big, blustery and easily outwitted.

moral.lesson: Think before you agree to a bargain. The hasty Bear chooses twice without asking what is being planted; the careful Peasant knows that tops or roots depends on the crop.
moral.reflectionQuestion: What should the Bear have asked before he said “Done!”?

moral: Think and ask before you agree to a bargain.

cover.alt: A peasant holding up a round turnip and a big brown bear holding a bunch of green leaves, side by side in a field.

card.label: Character · in Part I and Part II
card.title: The Peasant
card.body: He has one field, one horse and one wooden plough. He knows what grows up and what grows down. When a bear roars at him, he takes off his cap and makes a plan.

portrait.alt: The Peasant in a red shirt and a cap, holding a round turnip by its leaves.

card.label: Character · in Part I and Part II
card.title: The Bear
card.body: He says the forest is his, and he roars a great deal. But he would much rather eat than fight. He says “Done!” before he has asked a single question.

portrait.alt: The big brown Bear sitting down, chewing a green turnip leaf and looking puzzled.

tapTargets.line: A wide land of trees: white birch, tall pine and dark spruce.

cultureNote.label: From Russia
cultureNote.text: Russia has more forest than any other country. Bears still live among its trees.

cultureNote.label: From Russia
cultureNote.text: Turnips grow fast, even in a short, cool summer. Long ago, Russian village families ate them often.

framingDevice.label: LONG AFTER THIS STORY
framingDevice.line: Round as onions! Long after this story, builders in Russia gave a great building roofs shaped like onions.

tapTargets.line: A tall grass whose seeds are ground into flour for bread.

cultureNote.label: From Russia
cultureNote.text: Rye grows well in cold places. Russian bakers make a dark, rich loaf from it, called black bread.

runs.t: At the edge of a great
forest
lived a poor
Peasant
runs.name: peasant

runs.t: A peasant is a farmer who owns very little. This one had one field, one horse and one wooden plough.
One spring morning he went out to plough. The earth turned over, dark and soft, and the birds sang in the birch trees.

unfolded.alt: A spring morning at the edge of a forest of birch and spruce. A peasant in a red shirt ploughs dark earth with a small horse, and a big brown bear steps out of the trees.

folded.alt: A big brown bear steps out of the birch trees towards a peasant and his horse.

runs.t: Crack!
went the bushes. Out of the forest came a great brown
Bear
runs.name: bear

runs.t: “Peasant!”
he roared.
“This is my forest. I will break you up like a stick!”
The horse stopped. The birds stopped. But the Peasant did not run. He took off his cap.

unfolded.alt: A spring morning at the edge of a forest of birch and spruce. A peasant in a red shirt ploughs dark earth with a small horse, and a big brown bear steps out of the trees.

folded.alt: A big brown bear steps out of the birch trees towards a peasant and his horse.

runs.t: “Don’t, Bear,”
he said.
“Let us share. I will do the sowing. When the crop is ripe, you take the tops, and I will take only the roots.”
The Bear scratched his ear. Tops were on top. Tops must be best.
He did not ask what the Peasant was sowing.
“Done!”
he said, and he ambled back into the trees.

unfolded.alt: A spring morning at the edge of a forest of birch and spruce. A peasant in a red shirt ploughs dark earth with a small horse, and a big brown bear steps out of the trees.

folded.alt: A big brown bear steps out of the birch trees towards a peasant and his horse.

runs.t: Summer is short in the north, so the Peasant did not waste a day.
He sowed. He weeded. He chased away the crows.
Up came the leaves, thick and green. Now and then the Bear came by to look.
“My tops are growing nicely,”
he said.

unfolded.alt: An autumn field under yellow birch trees. A peasant loads a wooden cart with round turnips, and a bear sits beside a heap of green leaves.

folded.alt: A bear sits by a heap of green leaves and looks at a cart full of round turnips.

runs.t: Autumn came. The birch leaves turned yellow, and the Bear came for his share.
The Peasant took hold of some leaves and pulled.
Pop!
Out of the dark earth came a
turnip
, fat and white. Then another, and another.
He cut off the green tops and made a heap.
“Yours, Bear. Just as we agreed.”

unfolded.alt: An autumn field under yellow birch trees. A peasant loads a wooden cart with round turnips, and a bear sits beside a heap of green leaves.

folded.alt: A bear sits by a heap of green leaves and looks at a cart full of round turnips.

runs.t: The Bear sat down by his heap of leaves. He chewed one. It was tough. It was bitter.
The Peasant loaded his cart. In went the turnips, round as
onions
, until the cart was full.
The Bear stopped chewing.
“What have you got there, Peasant?”

unfolded.alt: An autumn field under yellow birch trees. A peasant loads a wooden cart with round turnips, and a bear sits beside a heap of green leaves.

folded.alt: A bear sits by a heap of green leaves and looks at a cart full of round turnips.

runs.t: “Only my roots, Bear. I am taking them to town to sell.”
“Give me one to try.”
The Peasant tossed him a turnip, and the Bear bit it in two.
Crunch!
It was sweet. It was juicy. It was much, much nicer than leaves.

unfolded.alt: An autumn field under yellow birch trees. A peasant loads a wooden cart with round turnips, and a bear sits beside a heap of green leaves.

folded.alt: A bear sits by a heap of green leaves and looks at a cart full of round turnips.

runs.t: “Grrr!”
said the Bear.
“Your roots are sweet and my tops are bitter. Next year, I take the roots!”
“As you wish, Bear,”
said the Peasant.
“Next year the roots are yours, and I will take only the tops.”
The Bear nodded hard. Once again, he did not ask what would be sown.

unfolded.alt: A spring morning at the edge of a forest of birch and spruce. A peasant in a red shirt ploughs dark earth with a small horse, and a big brown bear steps out of the trees.

folded.alt: A big brown bear steps out of the birch trees towards a peasant and his horse.

runs.t: Next spring the Peasant ploughed his field again.
His
wife
runs.name: wife

runs.t: carried out a sack of seed.
“Turnips again?”
she asked.
“Not this year,”
said the Peasant.
“This year we sow
rye
And he scattered the grain by the handful, left and right.
Far off in the trees, the Bear rubbed his paws.
“My roots,”
he said.
“My sweet, sweet roots.”

unfolded.alt: High summer. A wide field of tall golden rye under a pale blue sky, with a bear standing at its edge, watching it grow.

folded.alt: A bear peers over a field of tall golden rye.

runs.t: The rye came up green. All summer it grew, up to the Peasant’s knee, up to his belt, up to his shoulder.
Then it turned gold, and it whispered when the wind blew.
Every day the Bear came to look.
“Grow, roots, grow,”
he sang. He never once looked at the tops.

unfolded.alt: High summer. A wide field of tall golden rye under a pale blue sky, with a bear standing at its edge, watching it grow.

folded.alt: A bear peers over a field of tall golden rye.

runs.t: At harvest time the Peasant came with his sickle, a knife curved like a new moon.
Swish, swish, swish! Down fell the golden rye. His wife tied it into sheaves, and they stacked the sheaves on the cart.
“Now, Bear,”
said the Peasant,
“the roots are yours. Every one.”

unfolded.alt: Harvest time. A peasant stands by a cart of golden sheaves and full sacks, and a bear sits on a heap of dry roots. Far off are a log house and a village.

folded.alt: A bear sits on a heap of dry roots beside a cart stacked with golden sheaves.

runs.t: The Bear dug. He pulled up a root, thin and dry as string. He chewed it. He pulled a face.
“Peasant!”
he roared.
“Tops, and I get leaves. Roots, and I get string! How do you do it?”
“I don’t do it, Bear. The crop does. Turnips grow down. Rye grows up. You never asked what I was sowing.”

unfolded.alt: Harvest time. A peasant stands by a cart of golden sheaves and full sacks, and a bear sits on a heap of dry roots. Far off are a log house and a village.

folded.alt: A bear sits on a heap of dry roots beside a cart stacked with golden sheaves.

runs.t: The Bear sat on his heap of roots and thought for a long time.
In the village, the Peasant’s wife baked black bread from the new rye. The whole house smelled of it.
Before the first snow, the Peasant carried a warm loaf and a basket of turnips to the edge of the forest. He left them on a stump.

unfolded.alt: Harvest time. A peasant stands by a cart of golden sheaves and full sacks, and a bear sits on a heap of dry roots. Far off are a log house and a village.

folded.alt: A bear sits on a heap of dry roots beside a cart stacked with golden sheaves.

runs.t: The Bear found them. He ate the loaf. He ate the turnips. He licked the basket.
“Next spring,”
he said, with his mouth full,
“I will not say tops, and I will not say roots. I will say: Peasant, what are we planting?”
Then he yawned a great yawn, and went off to sleep until spring.
